title: Office Supplies Company: journalizing a credit sale and an accrued expense, revenue recognition and ethics of net-income bonuses
participant_role: Controller at OFFICE SUPPLIES COMPANY clarifying how two October transactions affect net income
judge_role: Vice president of OFFICE SUPPLIES COMPANY who received a bonus complaint from the sales and marketing manager
scenario:
You are to assume the role of the controller at OFFICE SUPPLIES COMPANY. The vice president of the company (judge) wants you to clarify transactions.

The sales and marketing manager at the company earns a monthly bonus based on net income. The manager is not happy with the bonus received for October. The manager has complained to the vice president (judge) about the bonus. The manager believes that you are not correctly calculating net income. The vice president (judge) has asked to meet with you for clarification of specific transactions of interest. The transactions are listed below.
a. On 10/31 the manager made a sale of 500 ink cartridges on credit for $50 each at a cost of $30 each. The ink cartridges shipped to the customer on 11/1.
b. Received an invoice for Web hosting fees of $500 for the month of October due November 15.

You are to:
- Explain how each transaction is journalized
- Explain how each transaction affects net income on the October Income Statement
- Discuss ethical considerations related to basing bonuses on net income

You will present your ideas to the vice president (judge) in a role-play to take place in the vice president's (judge's) office. The vice president (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented ideas and have answered the vice president's (judge's) questions, the vice president (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Why is it important to offer bonuses or incentives to our sales team?

solution.overview: A strong answer journalizes the cartridge sale as Accounts Receivable $25,000 to Sales and Cost of Goods Sold $15,000 to Inventory, but explains that under the revenue recognition principle the sale is not earned until the goods ship on 11/1, so it adds nothing to October net income. The $500 web hosting invoice is an October expense (matching principle) recorded as an expense and Accounts Payable, so it lowers October net income even though it is paid in November. It then explains that net-income bonuses encourage cost control but tempt managers to ship early or delay expenses, so controls and ethics matter.

answer: Transaction a: 500 cartridges x $50 = $25,000 of sales; debit Accounts Receivable 25,000, credit Sales 25,000
Transaction a also records the cost: 500 x $30 = $15,000; debit Cost of Goods Sold 15,000, credit Inventory 15,000
These entries are dated when the sale is earned, which is the shipping date 11/1, not 10/31
Transaction b: debit Web Hosting (or Marketing) Expense 500, credit Accounts Payable 500, recorded in October when the invoice is received
When the invoice is paid on November 15: debit Accounts Payable 500, credit Cash 500
Transaction a does not affect October net income because the cartridges were not shipped until November
The revenue recognition principle says revenue is recorded when earned; here it is earned when the goods ship, so the $25,000 sale and $15,000 cost belong to November
The $10,000 gross profit on the sale will raise November net income, and the manager's November bonus, instead
Transaction b: expenses are recorded when incurred, and the hosting fee is for October, so the $500 is an October expense even though it is paid November 15
Net income = revenue - expenses, so the $500 reduces October net income
The income statement reports revenue and expenses for a period, so timing decides which month each item belongs to
Basing bonuses on net income is better than basing them on revenue because it encourages managers to control costs too
But both methods create temptation to manipulate results: a manager might ship items before a real order exists to book revenue early
A manager might also push expenses into future periods to inflate the current month's net income
The controller must apply GAAP consistently (revenue recognition, matching) regardless of bonus pressure, and the company should have review controls and a clear bonus policy
Explaining the rules to the manager now prevents future disputes and protects the accuracy of the financial statements

judge_question_answers.question: Why is it important to offer bonuses or incentives to our sales team?
answer: Bonuses motivate the sales team to bring in more revenue and, when tied to net income, to sell profitably and watch costs
They help attract and keep good salespeople, since pay rises with performance
They align employee goals with company goals, as long as the measure is calculated fairly and consistently

judge_question_answers.question: Is bonus money taxed?
answer: Yes; a bonus is taxable wages to the employee, subject to federal and state income tax withholding and Social Security and Medicare taxes
The company also owes its share of payroll taxes on the bonus and reports it on the employee's W-2
The bonus is a deductible payroll expense for the company

key_concepts.definition: Recording a business transaction in the journal as a debit and credit entry, with debits always equal to credits.
Revenue is recorded when it is earned, which for a product sale is when the goods are delivered or shipped to the customer, not when the order is taken or cash is received.
Expenses are recorded in the period they are incurred to help earn revenue, even if paid later. October's web hosting fee is an October expense.
Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred rather than when cash changes hands; required by GAAP.
An asset showing amounts customers owe for sales made on credit.
A liability for bills the company has received but not yet paid, such as the $500 hosting invoice due November 15.
The cost of the inventory that was sold; recorded with a debit to COGS and a credit to Inventory at the same time as the sale.
Sales minus cost of goods sold. Gross profit = Sales - COGS; here $25,000 - $15,000 = $10,000.
Revenue minus expenses for a period; the bottom line of the income statement. Net income = Revenue - Expenses.
The financial statement that reports revenue, expenses and net income or loss for a specific period, such as the month of October.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the rules, such as revenue recognition and matching, that make financial statements consistent and comparable.
Manipulating reported net income, for example by shipping goods before a real order or delaying expenses, to hit a target or earn a bonus; it is unethical and violates GAAP.
